name: Highlands

verification.previous: V2 (research/area-verification-V2.md; all local facts were unverified because www.highlands.ca was blocked)

facts.text: Highlands' Tree Management Bylaw No. 10 (1994) needs a tree cutting permit to remove a protected tree or any tree near a watercourse, lake or steep slope, and prohibits cutting a significant tree. Significant trees are specific trees the bylaw lists in its Schedule A, not a size class.
facts.excerpt: A tree cutting permit is necessary when removing a protected tree or any tree located near a watercourse, lake, or steep slope area.
facts.note: V3: confirmed on the live page (https://www.highlands.ca/node/133 redirects here). The old excerpt dropped a word; the page reads 'Cutting down a significant tree is strictly prohibited.' Bylaw s.8(a) and (c), verbatim: 'The trees identified on Schedule "A" attached hereto are hereby designated as "Significant Trees"' and 'No person shall cut down a significant tree designated as such under section 8(a) of this by-law.' The bylaw PDF is an office consolidation 'for convenience purposes only' that 'includes amendments up to October 15, 2001' and 'may or may not contain the latest amendment (s)'; tell readers to confirm with the District.

facts.text: Highlands lists Garry oak, arbutus, Pacific dogwood, Pacific yew, cascara and manzanita as protected trees, plus Douglas-fir over 60 cm in diameter and any tree over 80 cm in diameter. The bylaw defines a tree as a woody plant 5 m or taller or 10 cm or more in diameter, with diameter measured 1.4 m above the ground.
facts.excerpt: Douglas Fir tree (Pseudotsuga menziesii), having a diameter greater than 60 centimetres (24 inches)
facts.note: V3: confirmed on the live page, INCLUDING the thresholds in content/areas/highlands.json (Douglas-fir over 60 cm, any tree over 80 cm), which V2 could not check. Same page, verbatim: 'Any tree having a diameter greater than 80 centimetres (31.5 inches)'. The old excerpt 'Under the Tree Management Bylaw protected trees are:' is also on the page but carries no threshold. Tree definition and 1.4 m measurement: bylaw s.1(k) and s.2. The bylaw PDF is an office consolidation 'for convenience purposes only' that 'includes amendments up to October 15, 2001' and 'may or may not contain the latest amendment (s)'; tell readers to confirm with the District.

facts.text: Under Highlands' tree bylaw, 'cut down' includes topping a tree and removing any branch or trunk over 10 cm in diameter, so that kind of pruning on a regulated tree is treated like cutting and needs a permit. Damaging roots inside the drip line, placing fill or materials there, running heavy equipment over the roots, removing soil or blasting near the roots also need a permit first.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Management Bylaw No. 10, 1994 (office consolidation to October 15, 2001), District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: includes the topping of a tree and the removal of any branch or trunk of a tree having a diameter of more than 10 centimetres
facts.note: V3: NEW (s.1(c) 'Cut Down' and s.9(a) tree damaging activities). s.9(a), verbatim: 'No person shall carry out or allow to be carried out any of the following tree damaging activities unless a permit to do so is first obtained'. The list includes 'Operating trucks, backhoes, excavators or other heavy equipment over the roots of a tree growing inside the drip line' and 'Removing soil from land inside the drip line of a tree'. The bylaw PDF is an office consolidation 'for convenience purposes only' that 'includes amendments up to October 15, 2001' and 'may or may not contain the latest amendment (s)'; tell readers to confirm with the District.

facts.text: In Highlands, cutting any tree needs a permit within 30 m of Millstream Creek or 15 m of any other watercourse, and within 30 m of Teanook, Matson, Fizzle, Fork, Eagles, Mitchell, Second, Third or Pease Lakes or 15 m of any other lake.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Management Bylaw No. 10, 1994 (office consolidation to October 15, 2001), District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: growing within 30 metres of the natural boundary of Millstream Creek or within 15 metres of any other watercourse
facts.note: V3: NEW (s.5 Watercourses, s.6 Lakes). s.6, verbatim: 'growing within 30 metres of the natural boundary of Teanook, Matson, Fizzle, Fork, Eagles, Mitchell, Second, Third or Pease Lakes or within 15 metres of the natural boundary of any other lake.' The District's riparian page separately applies a 30 m test to earthworks and tree removal near ANY watercourse (highlands-riparian-30m), so use 30 m as the safe planning figure. The bylaw PDF is an office consolidation 'for convenience purposes only' that 'includes amendments up to October 15, 2001' and 'may or may not contain the latest amendment (s)'; tell readers to confirm with the District.

facts.text: Highlands' tree bylaw needs a permit to cut more than 2 trees a year on a steep slope (an average slope over 30% across 6 m), and stumps and roots on steep slopes may not be removed without written permission. As consolidated, it also needs a permit to cut any tree within 20 m of a lot line along a road, trail or right-of-way, or within 10 m of any other lot line.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Management Bylaw No. 10, 1994 (office consolidation to October 15, 2001), District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: No person shall, without first obtaining a tree cutting permit, cut down more than 2 trees in any one calendar year growing on any steep slope
facts.note: V3: NEW (s.7 Steep slope areas, s.1(j) 'Steep Slope', s.3(e) buffer areas). s.3(e), verbatim: 'cut down any tree in the following designated buffer areas: i) within 20 metres of any lot line adjacent to or abutting a highway or road, or trail, right-of-way; or ii) within 10 metres of any other lot line.' The tree page does not mention the lot-line buffers, so write 'check with the District before cutting near a property line' rather than stating the buffers as settled. The bylaw PDF is an office consolidation 'for convenience purposes only' that 'includes amendments up to October 15, 2001' and 'may or may not contain the latest amendment (s)'; tell readers to confirm with the District.

facts.text: Highlands reports a fast-rising number of dead and dying Douglas-fir and cedar trees linked to drought and heat stress. Removing a dead or dying tree may still need a permit under the tree bylaw or a development permit area, and land title covenants can add limits. The District advises checking for nesting birds before felling, and chipping or mulching instead of burning.
facts.excerpt: A permit may be required under the Highlands Tree Management Bylaw or Development Permit Area and restrictions may apply under land title covenants.
facts.note: V3: NEW. Same page, verbatim: 'Before falling a tree, check for nesting birds in the tree or in nearby ground cover during nesting seasons' and 'Chipping and mulching are highly valuable forms of keeping the carbon close to the soil'. Bylaw s.13(b): no charge for a permit for a dead, dying or hazardous tree. Pairs with regional-bc-wildlife-act-nests.

facts.text: Highlands has six development permit areas: Steep Slopes, Water and Riparian Areas, Sensitive Vegetation, Regenerative Development, Intensive Residential, and Energy and Water Conservation and Reduction of Greenhouse Gases. Inside one, a development permit is needed before subdividing or before building, adding to or altering a building. Whether a lot is in one depends on what is on the ground, usually confirmed by a qualified professional.
facts.sourceTitle: Development Permit Areas | District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: The determinant for whether an area is subject to a development permit will be dictated by what is on the ground.
facts.note: V3: CORRECTED source and list. The old sourceUrl (Development Permit 1-5 - Jan 2024 PDF) is the DP APPLICATION FORM, and the old excerpt is not in it; the DPA list and the 'what is on the ground' rule are on this page. Same page, verbatim: 'Within a DPA, a property owner must obtain a development permit before subdividing land or constructing, adding to, or altering a building.' and 'Typically, this has to be verified by an appropriately qualified professional.' The 2024 form lists blasting, vegetation removal, tree cutting, soil deposit or removal and site grading as DPA activities, and the tree permit form says tree cutting inside a DPA also needs a development permit. OCP s.11.2 (General Policies 5(a) and 6) lists exemptions only for minor modifications to existing buildings, agency habitat work, managed forest land and emergencies; no gardening exemption was found.

facts.text: In Highlands, earthworks or tree removal within 30 m of any watercourse or water body, whatever its size, needs a Qualified Environmental Professional and the District's Water and Riparian Areas development permit; soil deposit or removal sends the application to Council. Installing a structure, including a fence, within 30 m needs a development variance permit under section 3.3 of the Zoning Bylaw.
facts.sourceTitle: Riparian Area Regulations | District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: If you plan to undertake earthworks or construction within 30 meters (approximately 100 feet) of any watercourse or water body, regardless of its size
facts.note: V3: NEW. Same page, verbatim: 'all of which require you to hire a Qualified Environmental Professional' and 'Section 3.3 of the Zoning Bylaw contains regulations regarding installing structures (including a fence) within 30m (approximately 100 feet) of water and riparian areas.' The variance process 'typically takes 2 Council meetings'. OCP Map 11.1 'generally shows - but does not capture all - water and riparian areas'.

facts.text: Most Highlands homes draw drinking water from private wells in a bedrock aquifer (BC Aquifer #680), so irrigation is planned around well yield. CRD watering rules apply only to the parts of Highlands on the Juan de Fuca system.
facts.sourceTitle: Groundwater Protection - Final Work Plan and Implementation Report (District of Highlands)
facts.excerpt: The majority of residents in the District obtain their drinking water from private wells that tap into the local bedrock aquifer (BC Aquifer #680).
facts.note: V3: confirmed on the live PDF; the excerpt now starts with the capital 'The' and includes the aquifer number, as in the PDF. Groundwater & Well Information page (https://www.highlands.ca/sustainability-and-climate-action/groundwater-well-information, node/150 redirects there), verbatim: 'most of the 2,100 residents rely on private wells for their potable water'. The District's 2017 brochure adds that piped water 'is prohibited by a CRD servicing agreement (urban containment boundary)' for most residents. 'Irrigation is planned around well yield' is our framing. CRD part: see regional-crd-water-systems ('parts of Highlands').

facts.text: Many Highlands wells are high in iron and manganese. The District's well pamphlet advises testing household taps at least once a year for coliform bacteria and every few years for metals, and its groundwater brochure says these minerals stain plumbing, dishes and laundry.
facts.sourceTitle: Caring for Your Well (District of Highlands pamphlet, 2024)
facts.excerpt: many wells in the Highlands are high in iron and manganese
facts.note: V3: CORRECTED. The old source (node/150) now redirects to the Groundwater & Well Information page, which does not carry the iron wording; it is in the 'Caring for your well' pamphlet linked from that page. The old text said 'test tap water at least yearly'; the pamphlet says yearly for coliforms and every few years for metals. The old inference that iron stains paving, siding and plants was REMOVED: the District's brochure (https://www.highlands.ca/sites/31/files/2025-02/2017%20Version%20%3D%20taking%20care%20of%20our%20water%20supply_201805241433132505.pdf), verbatim: 'These minerals stain plumbing, dishes and laundry'.

facts.text: In the District's 2025 monitoring, Highlands groundwater levels were highest in the wet months of December to April and fell to a seasonal low over the dry May-to-September period, the same months gardens need the most water.
facts.sourceTitle: Results of 2025 Groundwater Level Monitoring Program, District of Highlands (WSP, June 16, 2026)
facts.excerpt: declining to a seasonal low during the dry summer period from May to September
facts.note: V3: NEW. Same report, verbatim: 'Groundwater elevations were highest in the wet winter months of December to April'. The last clause is our framing. Do not quote well readings; the report is annual.

facts.text: The District's groundwater brochure asks residents to cut outdoor water use by replacing irrigated lawn with drought-resistant plants or letting lawns go dormant in summer, and, where they do irrigate, to use ground-level soakers instead of spray heads and water at night or early morning.
facts.sourceTitle: Taking Care of Our Water Supply (District of Highlands brochure, 2017 version)
facts.excerpt: Replace spray heads with ground-level soakers. Irrigate at night or early morning rather than in the heat of the day.
facts.note: V3: NEW. Same brochure, verbatim: 'Reduce outdoor demand by replacing irrigated lawn areas with drought resistant plants (xeriscaping) and/or allowing lawns to dry out in summer'. The brochure says it was 'prepared by the Sustainable Land Use Select Committee and approved by Highlands Council'. Supports the drip-irrigation blurb in content/areas/highlands.json.

facts.text: Highlands has no open burning season: a free permit is required for every outdoor fire, all year, including campfires and incinerators, and is issued online. Campfires up to 0.5 m x 0.5 m and open fires up to 1 m x 1 m are approved automatically; larger fires are approved by staff. Under Fire Control and Protection Bylaw No. 474 (2025), fires larger than a campfire may be lit only when the venting index is 'Good'.
facts.excerpt: These permits are mandatory year-round and are free of charge.
facts.note: V3: confirmed on the live page (node/149 redirects here). RESOLVED: the bylaw is 'Fire Control and Protection Bylaw No. 474, 2025', which repeals 'District of Highlands Emergency Services Bylaw No. 264, 2005' (bylaw PDF https://www.highlands.ca/media/1612, s.1 and the repeal section). The bylaw PDF says it was adopted on 8 December 2025; the Wood and Backyard Burning page says Council adopted it on December 9, 2025 (the public notice is dated Dec 9 2025). Same page, verbatim: 'There is no longer an "open season" for burning'.

facts.text: Highlands' fire bylaw requires any fire larger than 0.5 cubic metres to be at least 6 m from any building or property line and 1 m from shrubs, tall grass, fences or other combustibles; fires over 1 cubic metre have much larger distances (as written, 500 m from any residence or business and 15 m from combustibles). Garden refuse may be burned only as dry garden refuse under a permit, and construction waste never.
facts.sourceTitle: Fire Control and Protection Bylaw No. 474, 2025 (District of Highlands)
facts.excerpt: No person shall permit any fire larger than 0.5 metre cubed to be located within 6 metres of any building or property line
facts.note: V3: NEW (s.35 Distance requirement; s.33(b)-(d)). s.35 continues, verbatim: 'any fire greater than 1 metre cubed shall increase these distancing requirements to 500 metres from any residence or business'. The 500 m figure is quoted as written; ask the Fire Department (250-474-1773) before planning a large burn. s.33(d)(ii) lets the Fire Chief permit 'the burning of dry garden refuse'; s.33(c), verbatim: 'The burning of construction or demolition waste is prohibited.'

facts.text: Highlands says its wildfire risk is real and its terrain is challenging for both fire behaviour and evacuation. The District offers free, no-obligation FireSmart home assessments (250-474-1773 or firesmart@highlands.ca), and the first phase of its FireSmart program includes a Community Wildfire Resiliency Plan.
facts.excerpt: Book a Free Home Assessment with no obligations
facts.note: V3: CORRECTED. The old excerpt was a paraphrase. The '2009 Community Wildfire Protection Plan' is NOT on the current page and was removed; the page lists 'Community Wildfire Resiliency Plan' among its first-phase initiatives (this closes the V2 gap on the 2009 CWPP). Same page, verbatim: 'Wildfire risk in Highlands is real.' and 'Be mindful that the terrain in Highlands is challenging in terms of both fire behaviour and evacuations.' (node/105 redirects here.)

facts.text: Highlands' FireSmart guidance: within 1.5 m of the house, remove mulch, vegetation and stored items and choose non-combustible surfaces such as landscape rock; from 1.5 to 10 m, space out deciduous trees and shrubs, prune branches up to 2 m from the ground, keep grass under 10 cm and avoid conifers and firewood; from 10 to 30 m, keep volatile fuels to a minimum and increase spacing between tree crowns.
facts.excerpt: Remove flammable materials beside house (mulch, vegetation, stored items)
facts.note: V3: NEW. Same page, verbatim: 'Select non-combustible surface materials like landscape rock', 'Prune branches up to 2 metres from the ground', 'Keep grass under 10cm in length' and 'Increase spacing between tree crowns'.

facts.text: Groundwater in Highlands also supplies the Hanington Estates subdivision, through two communal supply wells, and Bear Mountain Golf Course irrigation draws on wells within Highlands.
facts.sourceTitle: Results of 2025 Groundwater Level Monitoring Program, District of Highlands (WSP, June 16, 2026)
facts.excerpt: Irrigation water for the Bear Mountain Golf Course (Bear Mountain) is sourced from groundwater wells located within the Highlands.
facts.note: V3: CORRECTED source. The old excerpt ('Hanington Estates subdivision is served by groundwater wells') is not verbatim in the 2018 report; the current 2025 report (linked from the Groundwater & Well Information page) has the same facts. Same report, verbatim: 'obtains water from a water system ("Hanington Estates Water System") that is supplied by two communal supply wells'. The 2018 report has the same wording.

facts.text: Scotch broom grows throughout Highlands. The District says it thrives in sunny, disturbed areas, can intensify wildfires and block road sightlines, and leaves seed that stays viable in the soil for 30 years. A community Broom Bash runs each Saturday in May at the Highlands Community Hall.
facts.excerpt: Scotch Broom can be found throughout the Highlands.
facts.note: V3: NEW; closes part of the soils/invasives gap. Same page, verbatim: 'Each Saturday in May the Broom Bash takes place at the Highlands Community Hall.' and 'produce seeds that remain viable in the soil for 30 years'. TIME-BOUND: check the event calendar each year.

facts.text: Highlands advises residents in bear country to plant non-attractant plants, use a bear-proof composter, pick fruit a few days before it ripens, clear fallen fruit, and keep lawns mowed and weeded, because grasses, dandelion and clover are natural bear foods. Mountain ash, blueberries, huckleberries and clover are named as strong bear attractants. Deer are also seen in neighbourhoods.
facts.sourceTitle: Wildlife Sightings and Information | District of Highlands
facts.excerpt: Keep lawns mowed and weeded (grasses, dandelion and clover are natural bear foods).
facts.note: V3: NEW; partly closes the deer gap (the page notes 'from time to time we may encounter Deer in our neighbourhoods' but gives no deer-specific guidance). Same page, verbatim: 'Plant non-bear attractant plants in your garden.' and 'Pick fruit a few days before ripe or before it becomes extra fragrant.' The page also lists dated bear sightings, which are time-bound.

gaps: Tree bylaw currency: the only bylaw PDF on the site is an office consolidation to October 15, 2001; later amendments may exist. Confirm thresholds and lot-line buffers with the District before publishing them as settled.
The Schedule A list of designated significant trees was not reviewed tree by tree.
Soils (thin soil over rock): no official source found.
Deer: the District only notes that deer are seen in neighbourhoods; no deer-management guidance found.
Fire bylaw adoption date: the bylaw PDF says 8 December 2025 and the web page says December 9, 2025.
